full_transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-30
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 37 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Head of ML, Hightower), Samir Patel (Platform Eng), Grace Kim (CTO)

Summary (auto): quick sync, qualification of self-serve path, discuss credits and time-to-first-token, collect infra constraints for pilot.

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro from redwood side, i'm maya, i'm the account lead, and with me is ethan our se.
00:10 Lena Ortiz: hi, lena here, excited to dig in. we are evaluating a few inference stacks to power a new assistant feature.
00:17 Grace Kim: hi, grace - just listening in, want to understand the ops and security implications.
00:22 Maya Chen: great. quick agenda — gather stack details, time to first token (ttft) expectations, hosted vs dedicated vs private options, and define next steps for a pilot. sound good?
00:29 Samir Patel: yep. also want to flag compliance requirements — SOC 2 and internal audit, and our preference for KMS integration for customer keys.
00:35 Ethan Brooks: totally understood. real quick, can you describe current infra? what cloud, orchestration, that sort of thing.
00:42 Lena Ortiz: we run on AWS, EKS clusters, some workloads on EC2. model training is in-house; inference is currently via a mix of managed endpoints and a tiny Triton fleet for special low-latency routes. approx traffic for prototype will be low — a few hundred requests per day — but target production is thousands per minute.
01:05 Maya Chen: cool. that makes sense. for a quickstart we usually recommend the hosted Redwood API, free credits to get you to first token — usually takes a dev an afternoon to integrate with our SDK. for benchmarks or heavy production you can move to dedicated reserved capacity or private VPC depending on isolation needs.
01:22 Lena Ortiz: quick question — what sort of ttft are we realistically looking at for a developer? like from sign-up to a successful call.
01:28 Ethan Brooks: for self-serve hosted, typical TTFT is under 2 hours for a simple hello world integration using our SDK and a public model. with streaming and proper request shaping you can get meaningful results in that window. getting full telemetry and per-route dashboards needs the console but that's setup is part of onboarding.
01:45 Samir Patel: ok. and how do you handle keys and encryption? we need customer-managed keys and audit logs.
01:50 Maya Chen: we integrate with customer K M S for Private deployments and Dedicated customers can bring K M S as well. hosted api supports envelope encryption and we provide rotation controls; for SOC 2 level audit logs we have an enterprise package or can enable longer retention for logs. i'll send the security pack.
02:06 Grace Kim: what about network isolation? do you support VPC peering or private link?
02:11 Ethan Brooks: yes — Private deployments support V P C connectors and on‑prem packages. Dedicated offers private endpoints and VPC options. Hosted by default is public API but we can configure private endpoints for enterprise contracts. there's a trade-off in terms of time-to-deploy vs isolation.
02:28 Lena Ortiz: latency — we need < 150ms p95 for short completions (<=64 tokens). is that achievable on hosted? we can tolerate some burst to dedicated but cost matters.
02:38 Ethan Brooks: p95 <150ms is achievable depending on model choice and sequence length. our benchmark page shows typical latencies for curated models. for consistent SLAs you'd look at Dedicated capacity where you reserve GPUs and get predictable throughput; hosted has higher variability but is fastest time-to-first-request. also batching can improve cost but adds latency — we can tune continuous batching to balance cost and latency.
03:05 Samir Patel: any built-in caching? we have many repeated prompts for certain flows.
03:10 Maya Chen: yes, prefix/K V cache is supported — it helps cut downstream token cost and latency for repeated contexts. we can enable caching at the route level.
03:17 Lena Ortiz: great. on pricing — are there credits for pilots? we prefer starting with free credits and then move to pay-as-you-go or reserved.
03:24 Maya Chen: we offer trial credits for PLG signups and additional pilot credits for sales-assisted pilots. i'll include the exact credit amount in the follow-up along with a pricing worksheet.
03:32 Grace Kim: compliance aside, are there any blockers for us? we have some procurement lead time and need S SO integration.
03:38 Ethan Brooks: S S O / SAML is supported in the console for RBAC. For audit we can export logs and provide SOC 2 artifacts. procurement timelines are pretty usual — pilot paperwork usually minimal for hosted, but Dedicated/Private has more procurement steps.
03:55 Lena Ortiz: one more technical — how do you handle KV cache eviction and memory footprint when we have long context windows?
04:03 Ethan Brooks: eviction policy is LRU by default, and the runtime manages kv shards; for very long sequences we'd recommend quantized weights and specific kernels — we can suggest models and quantization profiles based on payload distribution. part of the se work in the pilot is tuning those parameters.
04:25 Samir Patel: any direct competitor concerns? we've looked at Anthropic and some teams are leaning on in-house Triton for control.
04:33 Maya Chen: totally — self-hosted Triton gives control but you take on ops; Anthropic/OpenAI offer hosted simplicity but fewer deployment options. Redwood aims to bridge that with unified API plus dedicated/private options.
04:46 Grace Kim: log retention — legal wants 7 years of change history for some records, is that realistic?
04:52 Maya Chen: seven years is long; enterprise logs are configurable, we can discuss extended retention as part of enterprise add-ons. i'll include the retention options in the security doc.
05:05 Lena Ortiz: ok, let's talk concrete pilot. we'd like to run a latency and cost benchmark against our sample prompts and a 2‑week proof-of-concept on hosted first. if that looks good, we may request a dedicated reserved pool for production.
05:20 Ethan Brooks: perfect. proposed pilot: 2 weeks, Redwood provides X credits for the benchmark, we run tests with your sample dataset, we share a results spreadsheet with latency/cost breakdown by model/route, then we review findings and recommend a path (stay hosted vs move to dedicated/private).
05:38 Maya Chen: i'll coordinate credits and pricing and ethan will lead the benchmark. samir, can you share an infra diagram and a small sample of prompts and expected traffic patterns?
05:48 Samir Patel: yes, i'll put that in a doc and share by monday.
05:52 Lena Ortiz: timeline wise, we aim to start the pilot next week if legal ok's the trial form — procurement is about 2 weeks but pilot shouldn't need heavy paperwork.
06:02 Maya Chen: good. i'll send over the trial agreement and security pack today. we'll also include a quickstart guide that gets you from zero to first token in under 2 hours, with SDK examples in node and python.
06:14 Ethan Brooks: i'll also drop a benchmark runbook and a short script to replay sample prompts and capture p95/p99 latencies and token counts.
06:23 Grace Kim: anything else from redwood we need to see?
06:26 Maya Chen: just the security artifacts and the pricing sheet. any concerns on your side?
06:30 Lena Ortiz: not right now. main thing is we want a low-friction path to try hosted, but keep the door open to dedicated for predictable SLOs.
06:38 Maya Chen: understood. i'll follow up with docs and credits. thanks all.
06:42 Meeting end.

Notes on transcript: occasional transcription errors present (spaces in acronyms like V P C / K M S), proper nouns may be slightly off. Intent preserved.
